subject: Auto Body Repairs and Spray Painting

correct: Change out of overalls soaked with thinner before going near any heat or flame.

wrong.text: Spray a small 2K job in a dust mask because it will only take five minutes.
wrong.why: A dust mask stops particles, not isocyanate vapour. Even a short spray needs the proper respirator.

wrong.text: Wipe paint off your hands with thinner at the end of the day.
wrong.why: Thinner carries chemicals through the skin and dries it out. Wear nitrile gloves and use hand cleaner.

wrong.text: Throw thinner-soaked rags in the general dustbin by the door.
wrong.why: Soaked rags are a fire hazard. They go in the labelled rags container.

wrong.text: Keep a beard and test the respirator seal only when the mask feels loose.
wrong.why: Hair breaks the seal, so vapour leaks in. Seal-check every time you put it on.

wrong.text: Rinse used gun-wash thinner down the yard drain with plenty of water.
wrong.why: It pollutes the water and the fumes can build up. Collect it for recovery or proper disposal.

wrong.text: Leave a small oil spill until closing time, since everyone can see it.
wrong.why: Someone will slip on it. Clean a spill promptly with sawdust or dry sand.

wrong.text: Smoke outside the spray booth door with the door left open.
wrong.why: Solvent vapour drifts. No smoking or naked flames anywhere near the paint area.

distractors.name: Welding helmet
distractors.why: It protects against arc light. This job is about paint, dust and waste hazards.

distractors.name: Cotton nose mask
distractors.why: It stops neither fine dust well nor any vapour, so it gives false confidence.

distractors.name: Open plastic basin for thinner
distractors.why: Thinner must go in a labelled closed container, not an open basin.

distractors.name: Petrol for cleaning the floor
distractors.why: Petrol is a fire hazard. Spills are soaked up with sawdust or dry sand.

distractors.name: Leather sandals
distractors.why: They leave the feet open to falling tools and spills. Wear safety boots.

distractors.name: Sunglasses
distractors.why: They give no splash protection. Use goggles or a face shield.

decisions.prompt: You have put on the respirator. What do you do before entering the spray area?

options.text: Cover the inlets, breathe in gently and feel the mask pull in
options.consequence: The mask holds its seal, so you know vapour is passing through the cartridges only.

options.text: Breathe normally and go in if nothing smells bad to you after a minute
options.consequence: Many harmful vapours have little smell by the time they hurt you, and the leak goes unnoticed.

options.text: Tighten the top strap as hard as it will go
options.consequence: A strap pulled too hard can distort the mask, and you have still not tested the seal.

decisions.prompt: Engine oil has spread near the compressor. What do you do?

options.text: Cover with dry sand, sweep up and bin it in the correct container
options.consequence: The oil is soaked up and removed, so nobody slips and the waste stays controlled.

options.text: Wash it out of the door with a bucket of water
options.consequence: Oil floats on water, spreads further and ends up in the drain.

options.text: Wipe it up using a rag dampened with paint thinner from the spray shop
options.consequence: This adds a flammable solvent to the spill and leaves a soaked rag to deal with.

decisions.prompt: A tin holds used thinner, and another holds wet paint sludge. Where do they go?

options.text: Each into its own labelled container
options.consequence: Separated waste can be recovered or disposed of properly, and the labels warn others.

options.text: Both into one drum, to save space
options.consequence: Mixed waste cannot be recovered, so all of it becomes hazardous disposal.

options.text: Both left open outside so that they dry off
options.consequence: Vapour escapes into the air, and open tins can catch fire or spill.

decisions.prompt: The bench grinder's guard is cracked. What do you do?

options.text: Tag it, report it and keep it out of use
options.consequence: The tag warns everyone, and nobody is hurt before it is repaired.

options.text: Use it gently until the repairer comes
options.consequence: A cracked guard may fail without warning, and it can hurt you or a classmate.

options.text: Remove the guard so that it cannot rattle
options.consequence: The wheel is then fully exposed, which is more dangerous than before.

observations.prompt: You inspect the workshop at the end of the session. Which finding shows it is being kept safely?

options.text: Waste is separated and labelled, and the floor has no spills
Rags and sludge are stacked tidily in one open drum
options.why: Tidy is not the same as safe. Waste must be separated and closed in.

options.text: Thinner tins stand ready on the bench beside the grinder
options.why: Flammables belong in a metal cabinet, away from sparks.

options.text: All extinguishers are stored in the locked office
options.why: Extinguishers must be reachable at once, so they cannot be locked away.

numerics.prompt: A recycler recovers {p}% of {v} L of used gun-wash thinner. How many litres can be reused?
From {v} L of used thinner, {p}% is recovered. How many litres are left for hazardous disposal?
numerics.working: Recovered = {p} ÷ 100 × {v}. Left over = {v} minus that = {answer} L.

faults.scenario: Emeka's workshop was warned by an inspector after a spraying job. Here is what happened.

lines.text: He sprayed 2K paint wearing a dust mask.
lines.why: A dust mask does not stop isocyanate vapour.

lines.text: He poured the used thinner into the drain behind the shop.
lines.why: Thinner is hazardous waste. It goes for recovery or proper disposal.

lines.text: He kept using the same cartridges past their schedule.
lines.why: Old cartridges stop absorbing vapour. Replace them as scheduled.

lines.text: He stored his thinner in a metal cabinet.
lines.why: That is the right place for flammables.

lines.text: He cleaned an oil spill with dry sand.
lines.why: That is the safe way to deal with oil.

faults.scenario: Ngozi felt dizzy after spraying, although she wore a cartridge respirator. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She wore a respirator that was too big for her face.
lines.why: A poor fit lets vapour in around the edge.

lines.text: She skipped the seal check because she was in a hurry.
lines.why: The seal check is what shows a leak before you breathe the vapour.

lines.text: She kept her goggles and gloves on throughout.
lines.why: That protects the eyes and skin.

lines.text: She reported how she felt to the instructor.
lines.why: Symptoms must always be reported.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for using PPE and keeping the paint area safe.
written.explainPrompt: Why is a dust mask not enough when spraying 2K paint?
written.explainGuide: A dust mask only traps particles. The isocyanate in 2K paint is a vapour and mist that harms the lungs, so an air-fed or properly fitted respirator is needed.

board: Personal protective equipment and workshop housekeeping
Match each hazard to its protection.

correct: Disconnect a power tool before changing its disc or pad.

wrong.text: Blow dust off your overalls with the compressed air gun.
wrong.why: Compressed air can drive dust into the eyes or skin. Use a brush.

wrong.text: Carry the electric sander by its cable.
wrong.why: That damages the cable and its connection. Carry it by the body.

wrong.text: Keep sanding with a worn disc to finish the sheet.
wrong.why: A worn disc cuts unevenly and heats the panel. Change it.

wrong.text: Join a leaking air hose with tape and carry on.
wrong.why: A weak joint can burst or whip. Replace a damaged hose or coupling.

wrong.text: Lay a running sander down on the bench when you stop.
wrong.why: It can walk off the bench. Wait for it to stop before putting it down.

wrong.text: Leave the compressor tank undrained because the gauge reads normal.
wrong.why: The gauge does not show water. Water rusts the tank and spoils paint.

distractors.name: Claw hammer
distractors.why: It is a woodworking hammer. Its face would mark and stretch a panel.

distractors.name: Tenon saw
distractors.why: That is a woodworking saw, and no panel tool list has one.

distractors.name: Pipe wrench
distractors.why: It is a plumber's tool, and its jaws would mar body parts.

distractors.name: Wood rasp
distractors.why: A rasp is for wood. A body file is made for metal and filler.

distractors.name: Tin of grease
distractors.why: Grease on tools gets on panels and spoils paint. A light oil and a rag are used.

distractors.name: Spirit level
distractors.why: Panel shape is checked by hand, eye and file, not by level.

decisions.prompt: You are showing the hammer grip for panel work. How do you hold the bumping hammer?

options.text: Loosely, letting the wrist swing so that it rebounds
options.consequence: Light blows land where you aim, and the panel is not stretched.

options.text: Tightly near the head, for maximum control of the blow
options.consequence: A short tight grip gives heavy dead blows that leave marks.

options.text: At the very end, using a full arm swing
options.consequence: The blows are too hard and too inaccurate, so the metal stretches.

decisions.prompt: The tank drain valve spits rusty water when opened. What do you do?

options.text: Let it drain fully, then close it and note the check
options.consequence: The water is removed and the record shows when it was done.

options.text: Close it quickly so as to keep the pressure up
options.consequence: The water stays in the tank, causing rust and spoiled paint.

options.text: Add some oil to the tank to stop the rust
options.consequence: Oil in the air line contaminates paint and does not remove the water.

decisions.prompt: Your hammer face has a small chip. What do you do with it?

options.text: Set it aside and have the face dressed and polished
options.consequence: A polished face leaves no marks, so the panel needs no extra filling.

options.text: Use it for now, as filler will hide the marks
options.consequence: Every blow prints the chip on the panel, which costs extra time in filling.

options.text: Oil the face so it slides over the panel
options.consequence: Oil does not hide the chip, and it contaminates the surface.

observations.prompt: A student demonstrates a dolly. Which use is correct?

options.text: Held behind the panel while the hammer works the front
Struck on the panel face like a small hammer
options.why: A dolly is a backing tool, so this would dent the panel.

options.text: Used to lever a panel away from the frame
options.why: That is a job for a pry bar.

numerics.prompt: A sander needs {n} L/min of free air. The compressor delivers {c} L/min. What is the shortfall in L/min?
numerics.working: {n} − {c} = {answer} L/min, so this compressor cannot run the sander continuously.

faults.scenario: Tobi's repaired panel shows small marks and his paint has specks of water. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He kept using a hammer with a damaged face.
lines.why: Marks on the hammer transfer to the panel.

lines.text: He left water in the compressor tank for weeks.
lines.why: Moisture passes down the line and spoils the paint.

lines.text: He sanded with a worn disc to save money.
lines.why: A worn disc gives an uneven finish.

lines.text: He cleaned and oiled his tools after use.
lines.why: That is good maintenance.

lines.text: He stored his tools on a shadow board.
lines.why: That keeps them protected and easy to count.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for looking after body repair tools.
written.explainPrompt: Why must water be drained from the compressor tank regularly?
written.explainGuide: Air contains moisture that condenses in the tank. Left there, the water rusts the tank and passes down the line, which spoils paint work, so it must be drained.

board: Identifying and using body repair hand and power tools
Name it, use it, care for it.

correct: Keep the hardener cap on and the tube away from your eyes.

wrong.text: Dry-sand filler with no mask, as the dust settles quickly.
wrong.why: Filler dust is harmful to breathe. Wear the dust mask.

wrong.text: Mix the hardener in with bare fingers to feel the texture.
wrong.why: Hardener irritates skin. Wear gloves and use a spreader.

wrong.text: Wipe hardener from your eye area with a dirty rag.
wrong.why: That spreads it and can scratch the eye. Rinse with clean water and get help.

wrong.text: Blow filler dust off the panel using your mouth.
wrong.why: The dust goes into your eyes and lungs. Use a clean cloth or brush.

wrong.text: Scrape leftover mixed filler into the general bin while it is still curing.
wrong.why: Curing filler gets hot. Let it harden on the board, then dispose of it properly.

distractors.name: Paint brush
distractors.why: Filler is pressed on with a spreader. A brush cannot do it.

distractors.name: Wood glue
distractors.why: It is not a body filler and will not bond or sand like one.

distractors.name: P1200 wet and dry paper
distractors.why: It is far too fine for shaping filler and belongs to polishing.

distractors.name: Tin snips
distractors.why: Nothing is being cut out in this job.

distractors.name: Cement mortar
distractors.why: It is a building material, and it cracks and falls off a thin panel.

distractors.name: Wire brush for cleaning off paint
distractors.why: A wire brush does not take the area to clean bright bare metal as grinding does.

decisions.prompt: You have measured out filler. How much hardener do you add?

options.text: About 2% by weight, as the data says
options.consequence: The filler cures hard and sands well, with no staining.

options.text: A generous amount so that it sets faster
options.consequence: Too much hardener causes bleed-through staining in the paint.

options.text: A very small touch so that it stays workable
options.consequence: Too little hardener leaves soft, uncured filler that clogs paper.

decisions.prompt: The hardener is on the board. How do you mix it?

options.text: Fold and press with the spreader until the colour is even
options.consequence: An even colour means even curing, and no air gets folded in.

options.text: Whip it fast in a circle like an egg
options.consequence: Whipping beats in air, which shows later as pinholes.

options.text: Stir it briefly and leave some streaks showing in the filler
options.consequence: Uneven mixing leaves soft spots in the cured filler.

decisions.prompt: The dent still has old paint and a little rust. What do you do first?

options.text: Grind to bare metal and feather beyond the dent
options.consequence: Filler grips clean bare metal, so the repair will not lift.

options.text: Apply filler now, as it will seal the rust
options.consequence: Rust keeps growing under the filler and lifts it.

options.text: Scuff the paint lightly and spread on top
options.consequence: Filler over paint can peel with the old paint.

decisions.prompt: The filler has begun to set. When do you shape it with the body file?

options.text: At the cheesy stage, firm but not yet hard
options.consequence: The file cuts it cleanly, so little sanding is needed later.

options.text: Straight after spreading while it is soft
options.consequence: Soft filler drags and clogs the file and tears from the panel.

options.text: Next day, once it is rock hard
options.consequence: The file no longer cuts easily and you lose the easy shaping stage.

observations.prompt: The filler has cured and been sanded. Which result shows a good job?

options.text: Hard, smooth, flush with the panel and free from pinholes
Smooth but soft enough to mark with a fingernail
options.why: That means it is under-cured from too little hardener or poor mixing.

options.text: Hard, with small holes across the surface
options.why: Pinholes come from air whipped in. They need a skim coat.

options.text: Hard, and standing proud of the panel contour
options.why: It must be sanded down flush, or the repair will show.

numerics.prompt: Hardener is added at 2% by weight. How many grams of hardener do you need for {m} g of filler?

faults.scenario: Bola's filler repair has pinholes and soft patches, and it lifted after a month. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She whipped the filler quickly with the spreader.
lines.why: Whipping traps air, which leaves pinholes.

lines.text: She spread filler straight over rust.
lines.why: Filler must go on clean bare metal.

lines.text: She stopped mixing while streaks still showed.
lines.why: Uneven mixing leaves soft spots.

lines.text: She built the filler up in thin layers.
lines.why: Thin layers are correct, usually not over about 3 mm.

lines.text: She pressed the first layer firmly into the metal.
lines.why: That gives good adhesion.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for applying body filler.
written.explainPrompt: Why is filler folded and not whipped when mixing in the hardener?
written.explainGuide: Whipping traps air in the filler, and the air leaves pinholes in the cured surface. Folding and pressing mixes it evenly without air.

board: Mixing and applying body filler
Clean metal, thin layers.

correct: Bend the strip away from your face so that a sudden break cannot strike you.

wrong.text: Run your fingers along a freshly broken edge to feel the break.
wrong.why: Fresh edges are sharp. Wear gloves and look at the break instead.

wrong.text: Hold the small sample in your hand while you strike it.
wrong.why: The hammer can hit your hand. Hold it in the vice.

wrong.text: Strike the cast iron hard so it breaks in one blow.
wrong.why: Pieces can fly. The lesson calls for a gentle strike and steady force.

wrong.text: Leave your goggles off for a quick magnet and file test.
wrong.why: Filing and breaking can throw particles. Keep goggles on throughout.

wrong.text: Blow the filings off the sample and the bench.
wrong.why: Filings fly into your eyes. Use a brush.

distractors.name: Hydrometer
distractors.why: It measures liquid density, not the properties of a metal.

distractors.name: Multimeter
distractors.why: This job compares metals by magnet, bending and filing, not by electrical reading.

distractors.name: Plastic mallet
distractors.why: It cannot show malleability, which needs the steel hammer.

distractors.name: Paint thickness gauge
distractors.why: It reads coatings. This job tests the metal itself.

distractors.name: Wood chisel
distractors.why: It would be ruined on metal samples.

decisions.prompt: A silver-coloured panel does not attract the magnet. What do you conclude?

options.text: It is not steel, and may well be aluminium
options.consequence: The magnet test rules out steel, so you handle and repair it as a non-ferrous panel.

options.text: It is steel with a thick coat of paint
options.consequence: Check first, but do not assume. A thin coat does not stop a magnet on steel.

options.text: It is steel, since all silver panels are
options.consequence: Colour is no proof, and this is the common mistake the test is meant to prevent.

decisions.prompt: A sample's coating hides the metal colour. What do you do before comparing it?

options.text: File a small area to expose the bare metal
options.consequence: You now see and test the metal itself and not the coating.

options.text: Judge the metal by the colour of the coating
options.consequence: A coating can hide any metal, which is a known source of error here.

options.text: Mark it as steel and go on to the next
options.consequence: A guess gives a false record and spoils the comparison.

decisions.prompt: You bend the mild steel strip back and forth. What are you feeling for?

options.text: The metal growing stiffer near the bend
options.consequence: That is work-hardening, and it is what this step sets out to show.

options.text: The metal growing softer near the bend
options.consequence: That is the opposite. Softening comes from annealing, not from bending.

options.text: The strip stretching longer at each bend
options.consequence: The aim is to feel the stiffness change, not to measure length.

observations.prompt: Which result of the magnet test is correct?

options.text: Steel and cast iron attract it; aluminium, copper and brass do not
All the shiny samples attract it
options.why: Shine says nothing about magnetism: aluminium is bright and non-magnetic.

options.text: Only mild steel attracts it
options.why: Cast iron is ferrous too, so it also attracts.

options.text: Copper and steel attract it, but cast iron, aluminium and brass do not
options.why: Neither copper nor brass is magnetic.

observations.prompt: You strike a small piece of cast iron gently. What do you expect?

options.text: It cracks or breaks rather than bends
It bends slowly without cracking
options.why: That is how mild steel behaves. Cast iron is brittle.

options.text: It flattens out like copper
options.why: Copper is malleable, but cast iron is not.

numerics.prompt: A steel bonnet skin is 0.8 mm thick and {a} m² in area. Steel has a density of 7 850 kg/m³. What is its mass in kg?
numerics.working: Mass = thickness in metres × area × density = 0.0008 × {a} × 7 850 = {answer} kg.

numerics.prompt: An aluminium skin is 1.2 mm thick and {a} m² in area, with a density of 2 700 kg/m³. What is its mass in kg?

faults.scenario: Sade's table of metals has several errors. Here is what she did.

lines.text: She recorded a silver panel as steel without using the magnet.
lines.why: Not all silver-coloured panels are steel.

lines.text: She tested a painted sample without exposing the metal.
lines.why: Coatings hide the metal.

lines.text: She hit the cast iron hard with a full swing.
lines.why: Use small samples and steady force.

lines.text: She filed each sample to compare hardness.
lines.why: That is the planned test.

lines.text: She wore goggles when bending samples.
lines.why: That is required.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for testing metal samples.
written.explainPrompt: Why does a mild steel strip become stiffer near the bend before it breaks?
written.explainGuide: Repeated bending work-hardens the metal: its structure is deformed, so it becomes harder and less ductile until it cracks.

board: Identifying metals and demonstrating their properties
Test the metal, not its colour.

correct: Treat every piece of steel on the bench as hot until you have checked it.

wrong.text: Pick up the strip with bare hands once the glow has gone.
wrong.why: Steel stays hot long after it stops glowing. Use tongs.

wrong.text: Heat a spot near the fuel tank if the tank is nearly empty.
wrong.why: An almost empty tank still holds vapour. Keep heat well away from it.

wrong.text: Leave the seat and trim in place while heating the panel behind them.
wrong.why: Trim catches fire and smoulders. Remove it or keep heat away.

wrong.text: Quench with a dry rag to avoid steam.
wrong.why: A dry rag can scorch and it does not cool the spot. Use a wet rag.

wrong.text: Work without goggles, since the flame is only a small one.
wrong.why: Gas goggles protect your eyes from glare and sparks at any flame size.

wrong.text: Lay the lit torch on the bench while you pick up the hammer.
wrong.why: A lit torch can burn anything it points at. Use the proper rest or shut it off.

distractors.name: Bucket of engine oil on the bench
distractors.why: It is a fire hazard here. This job quenches in the water tank or with a wet rag.

distractors.name: Soldering iron
distractors.why: It cannot bring steel to red heat.

distractors.name: Plastic mallet
distractors.why: It would melt or mark on hot metal. Use the hammer and dolly.

distractors.name: Thermometer
distractors.why: Heat here is judged by the colour of the steel.

distractors.name: Spray gun
distractors.why: No paint is applied in this job.

decisions.prompt: The strip has reached dull red for annealing. How do you cool it?

options.text: Leave it to cool slowly in still air
options.consequence: Slow cooling leaves the steel soft, so it bends easily.

options.text: Plunge it straight into the water tank
options.consequence: On mild steel this does not give the slow cool that the process demands, so the comparison is spoiled.

options.text: Reheat it at once to a brighter red
options.consequence: More heat is not annealing, and you risk damaging the strip.

decisions.prompt: The high-carbon strip is file-hard after quenching. What comes next?

options.text: Temper it, then compare the toughness
options.consequence: Tempering takes away some brittleness while keeping useful hardness.

options.text: Bend it to see how hard it is
options.consequence: Hardened strip is brittle and may snap and fly.

options.text: Anneal it to make it harder still
options.consequence: Annealing softens steel and undoes the hardening.

decisions.prompt: A stretched bulge needs shrinking. What area do you heat?

options.text: A small spot, then tap it and quench it
options.consequence: The heat stays local, so the metal draws in without distorting the panel.

options.text: The whole bulge at one time
options.consequence: Heating too large an area distorts the panel.

options.text: The undamaged metal around the bulge
options.consequence: The stretched metal is what must be shrunk, so nothing is corrected.

decisions.prompt: The first spot is finished, and the bulge is 150 mm across. Where is the next spot?

options.text: Further round the bulge, working from the outside in
options.consequence: The stretch is drawn in step by step towards the centre.

options.text: On the same spot until it turns bright and starts to shrink
options.consequence: Repeated heat in one place risks burning through the thin panel.

options.text: Far away on another part of the panel
options.consequence: This leaves the bulge untouched and heats good metal.

observations.prompt: You test the quenched high-carbon strip with a file. What shows it has hardened?

options.text: The file skids and hardly cuts
The file cuts it as easily as mild steel
options.why: Then the strip has not hardened.

options.text: The strip bends under the file
options.why: Bending suggests a soft strip, not a hard one.

observations.prompt: After several shrinking spots, what shows success?

options.text: The bulge has drawn back level with the panel
A hole has opened at the centre of the spot
options.why: That is burn-through from overheating.

options.text: The bulge moved to the panel edge
options.why: That is distortion, not a repair.

faults.scenario: Kunle tried to shrink a bulge on a door skin, and the panel came out wavy with a small hole. Here is what he did.

lines.text: He heated an area as wide as his hand.
lines.why: Heating too large an area distorts the panel.

lines.text: He held the flame on one spot until it was very bright.
lines.why: Overheating burns through thin panels.

lines.text: He quenched a high-strength panel without checking if it allowed heat.
lines.why: Some high-strength steels are not designed for this.

lines.text: He tapped the spot down with hammer on dolly.
lines.why: That is the correct step.

lines.text: He kept a fire extinguisher at hand.
lines.why: That is a required precaution.

written.precautionsPrompt: State two precautions for heat-shrinking a panel.
written.explainPrompt: Why does a stretched panel need shrinking and not just hammering?
written.explainGuide: Stretched metal has too much surface area, so hammering only moves the bulge. Heating a small spot lets it upset and draw in as it cools, so the panel returns level.

board: Heat treatment of body metals
Small spots. Watch the colour.

correct: Stand to the side of the regulator when opening a cylinder valve.

wrong.text: Put a drop of oil on a stiff oxygen regulator thread.
wrong.why: Oil and oxygen together can ignite violently. Keep oxygen fittings free from oil.

wrong.text: Look for a gas leak with a lit match.
wrong.why: A flame can ignite the leak. Use leak detection fluid.

wrong.text: Lay the acetylene cylinder on its side so it cannot fall.
wrong.why: Cylinders must stand upright and be secured.

wrong.text: Light the blowpipe with a cigarette lighter from your pocket.
wrong.why: That brings your hand close to the flash. Use the spark lighter.

wrong.text: Leave out the flashback arrestors on a short hose run.
wrong.why: A flashback can happen on any length of hose. Fit the arrestors.

wrong.text: Wrap a leaking hose with tape and carry on welding.
wrong.why: Tape will not hold gas safely. Take the hose out of service and report it.

wrong.text: Carry a lighter in your overall pocket while welding.
wrong.why: Sparks and heat can set it off. Leave it out of the work area.

distractors.name: Arc welding electrode holder
distractors.why: That belongs to arc welding, and this job uses a gas flame.

distractors.name: Soapstone holder used as a lighter
distractors.why: It marks metal but makes no spark, so use the spark lighter.

distractors.name: Grease gun
distractors.why: Grease must never go near oxygen fittings.

distractors.name: Water hose for testing leaks
distractors.why: Leaks are tested with leak detection fluid, not by hosing the joints.

distractors.name: Large cutting nozzle
distractors.why: It is far too big for thin panel steel and would burn through.

distractors.name: Car jack
distractors.why: Nothing in this job needs lifting.

decisions.prompt: A regulator thread will not start on the acetylene cylinder. What do you do?

options.text: Check the thread direction, as fuel gas fittings are left-handed
options.consequence: The right fitting goes on without force, so the joint seals safely.

options.text: Force it with a longer spanner
options.consequence: Forcing damages the thread and makes a leak likely.

options.text: Use the oxygen regulator, since it fits the cylinder and saves time
options.consequence: Regulators are made for one gas, and swapping them is dangerous.

decisions.prompt: You are welding 0.8 mm panel steel. Which nozzle do you select?

options.text: Size 1, the smallest suitable nozzle
options.consequence: The heat is just enough, which limits distortion and burn-through.
